input x09 excerpt "Path-MTU probe pair" "## Path-MTU probe pair\n\nThe path-MTU probe pair is how the admission handshake learns whether a connection's path carries the connection's media packets whole: the source side sends a padded probe at the intended media packet size (C-116), the consumer side answers it with a small fixed-size reply, and a missing reply means the path is smaller (01-architecture.md § 3.3) `[decision]`. When the probe at the intended size gets no reply, the source side probes again at the 1 280-byte fallback (C-06), which is 1 252 bytes of UDP payload over IPv4 (C-17, C-100); when that probe gets no reply either, the handshake is refused with `PathMtuTooSmall` (C-173) `[decision]`. This section gives the pair its two codes in the block the Hello section reserves, lays out both messages, states their sizes, how a reply names its probe, the sequence and every invalid form with its outcome `[decision]`. It is not the one-way probe of the measurement layer (One-way probe), which measures delay between modules that already share an admitted connection; every name here says \"path-MTU probe\" to keep the two apart `[decision]`.\n\n### Exchange\n\nWho probes and in which direction `[decision]`: the source side probes and the consumer side answers. Media flows from the source to the consumer, so the forward path from the source side's pinned source address is the path whose size matters; the source side alone knows the intended packet size, which it puts in its admission request (Admission messages, Admission request), and the landed handshake already has the source side refuse an accepted handshake in turn with `PathMtuTooSmall` (Admission messages, Who sends what). The source side sends the first probe once it has sent its admission request, as 012-12 sends the request and the first probe together; the consumer answers every well-formed probe addressed to it when it receives it, whatever its own verdict on the request, so the probe and the request may cross on the wire in either order `[decision]`.\n\nAddressing and marking `[decision]`: a probe travels by UDP unicast over IPv4 (C-100), from the pinned source address the request states to the address and port the source side sends its admission messages to; the reply travels from the address the probe arrived on to the source address and port of the probe, the addressing a stateless reply needs, as the one-way probe uses (One-way probe, Exchange rules). Both messages are control messages at DSCP CS5 (40) (C-13), with the common control header (Hello, Common control header) and the C-12 authentication reservation at the v1 values of C-115: scheme 0, tag 128 zero bits and a live message counter, the sender's liveness counter (Hello, Liveness counter) `[decision]`.\n\nDon't-fragment (rule 11) `[decision]`: the sender sets the IPv4 don't-fragment bit on every probe and every reply, as on every packet of the protocol, and IP fragmentation is forbidden; without it a probe could arrive in fragments and prove nothing. An IPv4 datagram with the DF bit set is not fragmented: RFC 791, § 3.1 Internet Header Format, Flags: \"Bit 1: (DF) 0 = May Fragment, 1 = Don't Fragment\"; § 2.3: a datagram marked don't fragment that cannot be delivered without fragmenting \"is to be discarded instead\" `[standard]`. The protocol relies on that discard and on nothing else: it treats only the missing reply as the signal that the path is smaller, and it does not rely on an ICMP message reporting the drop, because on a switched path a too-small hop drops silently and silence is the answer only because a reply is expected (01-architecture.md § 3.3; 012-09) `[decision]`. The DF bit is in the IPv4 header, outside these messages, so no validity rule checks it; how a sender that cannot set it behaves is not specified anywhere in the design: the platform tickets 001-04, 001-09 and 021-03 test whether the bit can be set, and none says what a sender does when it cannot (Open item 6) `[decision]`.\n\nThe fallback sequence, in order `[decision]`:\n\n1. The first probe is sent at the request's intended packet size (C-116), or at 54 bytes, the probe's fixed part, when the intended size is smaller: a path that carries 54 bytes carries any smaller packet `[decision]`.\n2. If the intended packet size is above 1 252 bytes and the first probe gets no reply, the source side sends a second probe at the 1 280-byte fallback (C-06): 1 252 bytes of UDP payload, 1 280 bytes at the IP layer once the 20-byte IPv4 header and the 8-byte UDP header are added (Layer overview) `[decision]`.\n3. If the probe at the fallback also gets no reply, the source side refuses the handshake with `PathMtuTooSmall` (C-173), in an admission refusal carrying the request's request id (Admission messages, Admission refusal) `[decision]`.\n\nWhen the intended packet size is 1 252 bytes or less, the first probe is the only one: it is no larger than the fallback, so it is the probe at the fallback, and if it gets no reply the handshake is refused with `PathMtuTooSmall` `[decision]`. This is the reading 012-09 records (its AC 4: a first probe at or below 1 280 bytes counts as the fallback probe), and a second probe at 1 252 bytes would only test a size the connection never sends: the intended packet size is the largest media packet the source sends on the connection (Admission messages, Admission request), so a path that carries it carries every packet of the connection `[decision]`. This answers the Size budget's open item on the probe size (Size budget, Announcement schedule and omission rule): either the probe at the fallback carries 1 252 bytes of UDP payload with don't-fragment set, or the only probe carries the intended packet size, the largest media packet the connection sends, so no probe is sized below the connection's largest packet `[decision]`. The default slice is that case: it fits 1 252 bytes of UDP payload (C-137), so a path that passes the fallback probe carries the default slice, and every v1 default packet is at most 1 252 bytes (Size budget, Shared packets and the controller allowance) `[decision]`. What a reply proves, for the source side, is a lower bound only: a reply to a probe of intended packet size s shows that the path carries datagrams of at least s bytes of UDP payload, s + 28 bytes at the IP layer, in the direction the probe travels — from the source side to the consumer, the direction media flows — and nothing about how much larger a datagram it would carry, nor anything about the reverse direction beyond the reply's own 54 bytes (Path-MTU probe reply) `[decision]`. A reply to the first probe therefore means every packet of the connection crosses whole; a reply only to the probe at the fallback means the path carries 1 252 bytes of UDP payload but, as far as the pair shows, not the intended size, so a slice that no longer fits one packet travels in the explicit, stamped multi-packet regime (C-05; Slice header, Multi-packet regime); no reply to the probe at the fallback means `PathMtuTooSmall` `[decision]`. Which value, if any, the connection records as its path MTU is a separate question that this section does not answer: 013-07 stamps a `path_mtu` per connection and its AC 4 lowers one from 1 500 to 1 280, while 012-09 names an outcome per probe, and neither says how a recorded value derives from a lower bound (Open item 2) `[decision]`.\n\nHow many times a probe of one size is sent before it counts as unanswered, and how long the source side waits for a reply, are not wire fields and no constant gives them: 012-09 proposes a timeout as a pending-measurement parameter and sends one probe per size, and the probe retry timing is epic 005's, outside this ticket (Open item 1) `[decision]`. Where the result travels: in no admission message — the accept is the consumer's and carries no path MTU (Admission messages, Admission accept) — but in each side's regime stamp, which records the path MTU of each connection (01-architecture.md § 3.3; C-18), in a section no landed ticket of this epic lays out yet (Open item 2) `[decision]`.\n\n### Path-MTU probe request\n\nThe probe request is the padded probe, code 32 (Hello, Control message type codes). Little-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding for alignment (Alignment and padding); bytes 0 to 31 are the common control header, and bytes 32 to 51 are the three fields every admission message carries at those offsets — sender, recipient and request id (Admission messages, Common admission fields) — so one parser reads the handshake's addressing alike in all six messages `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured, ignored and counted (C-173) |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 32 = path-MTU probe request (Control message type codes) | 32 only |\n| 7 | 1 | u8 | Authentication scheme (C-12); 0 = none in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Message counter (C-12): live (C-115), the sender's data-plane liveness counter (Hello, Liveness counter) | any 64-bit value |\n| 16 | 16 | u128 | Authentication tag (C-12): 128 zero bits in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 32 | 8 | u64 | Sender module id (C-11): the source side's module id, the prober | any 64-bit value |\n| 40 | 8 | u64 | Recipient module id (C-11): the consumer module the probe is for | the receiving module's own module id |\n| 48 | 4 | u32 | Request id: the request id of the admission request whose path this probe tests (Admission messages, Common admission fields); with the intended packet size it identifies the probe | any 32-bit value |\n| 52 | 2 | u16 | Intended packet size: the UDP payload size this probe is sent at, and so the datagram's own size — the request's intended packet size for the first probe (C-116), or 54 when that is smaller; 1 252 for the probe at the fallback (C-06) | 54 to 65 507 |\n| 54 | 1 × max 65453 | pad | Padding: intended packet size − 54 bytes, which bring the datagram to the intended packet size; senders write zero (Reserved fields, General rule for later tickets) | 0 only; intended packet size − 54 bytes, at most 65 453 |"

input x10 excerpt "Regime stamp" "## Regime stamp\n\nThe regime stamp is a module's declaration of the configuration and health facts that peers and tools read to interpret its behaviour. C-18 sends it as a dedicated control message split into sections that each fit the control bound (C-17), multicast to the control group on any regime change and refreshed every 10 s, with a unicast request for an immediate fetch, and the hello carries only its version number (Hello, Regime stamp version number) `[decision]`. This section lays out the container — the stamp section and the stamp request, codes 36 and 37 of the block the Hello section reserves for 004-24 — fixes the maximum section count, the maximum stamp size and the storage a receiver needs, and states the sender rules, the receiver rules and every invalid form with its outcome `[decision]`. The section types, the bodies the container carries, are laid out by 004-25 (the types the constants table names) and 004-28 (observed DSCP and alignment group), and by later epics as minor changes, each epic that stamps state adding its own type (README of epic 004, gap R8) `[decision]`.\n\nBehaviour the layouts serve, restated as fact: both messages are control messages, sent by UDP over IPv4 (C-100) at DSCP CS5 (40) (C-13), and both start with the common control header and its C-12 authentication reservation at the v1 values of C-115 — scheme 0, tag 128 zero bits, and a live message counter that is the sender's liveness counter, one counter per module instance shared by every control message it sends, stamp sections and stamp requests included (Hello, Liveness counter) `[decision]`. Sections travel multicast to the control group with TTL 1, and unicast in answer to a request; the request travels by unicast only `[decision]`. The hosted backend sends the stamp (epic 015, C-144) on the schedule of 013-24, and a device sends it through epic 026 (013-24); this section fixes the bytes and the rules any sender and receiver follow, not the sending code `[decision]`. Third parties read stream health only from the stamps, since receiver reports are not multicast and there is no query message (C-47): the stamp request fetches a module's whole stamp, never a part of it and never a health query `[decision]`.\n\nThe retired POC has no regime stamp message: the only stamp its gossip carries is the transport reference's claim stamp, a u64 on the `transport` line of the text hello (module.rs:153, `pub stamp: u64` in `struct Info`, and module.rs:273, the `transport` line of `Info::hello`) `[code]`. No field of the container carries a timeline epoch, so the container adds no carrier to Election messages, Which carrier binds whom `[decision]`. Two section types of 004-25 do carry one, per stream: the multi-packet regime section the epoch 004-08 hands over, and the injections section the epoch a stream is forced onto (Section types of the constants table); 004-25 adds both to Which carrier binds whom as binding no one's adoption `[decision]`. 006-19 asks for a 16-bit timeline epoch per record set in the stamp, the epoch of the line in force when the records were taken, and leaves the section that carries it to epic 013 (006-19, Work 3; C-196); neither 004-25 nor 004-28 lays out that per-record-set field, so adding its carrier to Which carrier binds whom is owned by epic 013, which places the field, together with the epic-004 ticket that lays out its section type in this section `[decision]`.\n\n### Stamp section\n\nA stamp section carries one part of one version of the sender's stamp. Little-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding (Alignment and padding); bytes 0 to 31 are the common control header (Hello, Common control header), bytes 32 to 57 the section header, which names the stamp, the section's place in it and the body's type, and the body follows `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured, ignored and counted (C-173) |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 36 = regime stamp section (Control message type codes) | 36 only |\n| 7 | 1 | u8 | Authentication scheme (C-12); 0 = none in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Message counter (C-12): live (C-115), the sender's data-plane liveness counter (Hello, Liveness counter) | any 64-bit value |\n| 16 | 16 | u128 | Authentication tag (C-12): 128 zero bits in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 32 | 8 | u64 | Sender module id (C-11): the module whose stamp this section carries | any 64-bit value |\n| 40 | 8 | u64 | Instance nonce (C-11) of the sender: with the module id, the instance whose stamp this is, as in the hello | any 64-bit value |\n| 48 | 4 | u32 | Stamp version number (C-18): the version of the stamp this section belongs to, the hello's regime stamp version number | any 32-bit value |\n| 52 | 1 | u8 | Section index: this section's place in the stamp, counted from 0 | 0 to section count − 1 |\n| 53 | 1 | u8 | Section count: how many sections make up this stamp | 1 to 64 |\n| 54 | 2 | u16 | Section type: the code of the body's layout (Section type codes) | 1 to 65535; codes not assigned in v1 are skipped by their length |\n| 56 | 2 | u16 | Section length: how many body bytes follow | 0 to 1 194 |\n| 58 | 1 × max 1194 | u8 | Body: the section's typed content, laid out by the table of its section type (004-25, 004-28, later epics) | section length bytes, at most 1 194 |\n\nA stamp section's maximum size is 1 252 bytes: 32 + 8 + 8 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 58 bytes of header and at most 1 194 bytes of body, 58 + 1 194 = 1 252, exactly the control bound (C-17), as for the manifest section (Admission messages, Manifest section); a section with b body bytes is 58 + b bytes `[decision]`. The body follows the section length directly, and the section ends with the body's last byte `[decision]`.\n\nThe sender module id and the instance nonce name whose stamp a section belongs to, with the widths of the hello (C-11): the hello's staleness rule keys a copy by the pair (instance nonce, stamp version), so a section carries both, and a receiver matches it to a peer from its own bytes rather than from the datagram's source address, as a peer's hellos are matched by their module id and instance nonce `[decision]`. The stamp version number has the hello's width, 32 bits, and its two rules: a held copy is stale exactly when the pair (instance nonce, version number) of the peer's latest hello differs from the copy's, equality deciding within one nonce; and where an order is needed, versions of one instance nonce are ordered by serial comparison over half the range, v being newer than u exactly when (v − u) modulo 2^32 lies in 1 to 2^31 − 1, so a difference of 0 or 2^31 is never newer `[decision]`. This confirms Hello, Open item 6, whose owner is this ticket: its falsifier, a different width or comparison, does not hold `[decision]`.\n\nA receiver holds a complete stamp of one version when, for one sender module id, instance nonce and stamp version, it holds a section of every index from 0 to the section count − 1, each stating the same section count; this is the only completeness test, and no total length is carried `[decision]`. The section length equals the datagram size less 58; it is carried because it is what a receiver checks the body against and what it skips an unknown body by, as for an announcement or a content message (Versioning, Minor and major changes) `[decision]`. A section type may occupy several sections of one stamp — 004-25 and 004-28 split a type over several sections where its entries do not fit one — and one stamp carries sections of many types; whether a type may appear in more than one section, and how its entries are divided between them, is fixed by that type's own layout `[decision]`.\n\n### Section type codes\n\nThe section type is a u16 scoped to the regime stamp. Code 0 is never a section type, so a zeroed section header is never valid, and a block of codes is reserved for each epic-004 ticket that lays out section types, so tickets written in parallel cannot collide, as the Hello section reserves control message type codes `[decision]`:\n"

input x11 excerpt "Commissioning window messages" "## Commissioning window messages\n\nThe commissioning window is how the commissioning tool declares when it may drive test traffic: outside a declared window that every module stamps the tool is read-only (C-107); the tool announces the window on the control group with an expiry time, modules stamp it while it is open, and it closes at expiry or on explicit close (C-153) `[decision]`. This section gives the two messages codes 48 and 49 of the block the Hello section reserves for 004-29, lays out the window announcement and the window close, states their sizes, the receiver rules for the open, expiry and explicit-close transitions and for every other announcement or close a module can receive, and every invalid form with its outcome `[decision]`. Epic 004 owns the field layout and epic 005 the state machine that holds the window (C-228). The stamped form of the open window is the commissioning window section of the regime stamp (Regime stamp, Commissioning window section), laid out by 004-25, which this section fills and does not change: this section adds no regime stamp section type, so the section count and the condition on the connection cap (Regime stamp, Section count with the types of 004-28) are unchanged `[decision]`.\n\nBehaviour the layouts serve, restated as fact: both messages are control messages, sent by the commissioning tool by UDP over IPv4 (C-100), multicast to the control group with TTL 1, at DSCP CS5 (40) (C-13), and both start with the common control header and its C-12 authentication reservation at the v1 values of C-115, scheme 0 and tag 128 zero bits (Hello, Common control header) `[decision]`. A message of either kind that arrives by unicast is parsed by the same rules, as a hello is (Hello) `[decision]`. The announcement and the close are, with stamp requests, the only messages the tool sends outside a window (C-107; 028b-09, AC 4) `[decision]`.\n\nBoth messages carry the common control header's message counter as merged: live (C-115), the sender's liveness counter (Hello, Common control header; Hello, Liveness counter), any 64-bit value accepted `[decision]`. Two sends of one message may therefore differ in bytes 8 to 15, so every comparison of two announcements below runs from offset 32 to the end, as the regime stamp compares its sections (Regime stamp, Sender rules, rule 6) `[decision]`.\n\n**Reported contradiction: the liveness counter of a sender with no data plane.** The merged Hello row for offset 8 says that \"in every control message it is the sender's liveness counter (Liveness counter)\", the Stamp request row says \"the sender's data-plane liveness counter\", and C-115 says \"the 64-bit counter is live because it is the liveness counter\"; the Liveness counter rule defines it by the progress of the sender's data thread (Hello, Liveness counter). The commissioning tool is not a module: it sends no hello, has no entry in any discovery map and takes no part in a live data path (028a-01), yet it sends these two messages and stamp requests (028b-09, AC 4), so what its liveness counter counts is undefined in the design, and this section does not define it `[decision]`. In v1 no receiver depends on the tool's counter: the stall rule reads the counter across consecutive hellos of a peer in the discovery map (Hello, Liveness counter; 005-06), the tool sends no hello and has no entry there, and every value is valid, so a receiver of an announcement, a close or a stamp request accepts any value and acts on none `[decision]`. The contradiction is reported to the design owner and is Open item 8, with its owner and falsifier `[decision]`.\n\n### Window announcement\n\nThe window announcement, code 48 (Hello, Control message type codes), opens a window, or repeats or extends the window it names. Little-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding (Alignment and padding); bytes 0 to 31 are the common control header (Hello, Common control header) `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured, ignored and counted (C-173) |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 48 = commissioning window announcement (Control message type codes) | 48 only |\n| 7 | 1 | u8 | Authentication scheme (C-12); 0 = none in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Message counter (C-12): live (C-115), the sender's data-plane liveness counter (Hello, Liveness counter) | any 64-bit value |\n| 16 | 16 | u128 | Authentication tag (C-12): 128 zero bits in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 32 | 8 | u64 | Window identifier: drawn by the tool for this window and written unchanged in every announcement and close of it; the reference commissioning results carry (C-178) and the value the commissioning window section stamps (Regime stamp) | 1 to 18 446 744 073 709 551 615 (2^64 − 1); 0 is not a window identifier |\n| 40 | 8 | u64 | Tool identity: the identity of the commissioning tool that announces the window, the same in every announcement of the window | any 64-bit value |\n| 48 | 8 | u64 | Expiry time: the absolute instant at which the window closes, in nanoseconds of network time (timeline.md, Domain line and position map), one instant for every module | 0 to 9 223 372 036 854 775 807 (2^63 − 1) ns; 2^63 and above is out of range |\n\nThe announcement's maximum size, which is also its fixed size, is 56 bytes: 32 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 56, tiling bytes 0 to 55 with no gap, far within the 1 252-byte control bound (C-17) `[decision]`.\n\n**Window identifier.** The identifier is stable: the tool draws it once, when it opens the window, and writes it unchanged in every repeat and every extension of the announcement and in the close; every module stamps it verbatim in its commissioning window section (Regime stamp, Commissioning window section), and every commissioning result taken in the window records it (C-178; 028b-10 records a `window` in each sink and pair record), so one value names the window from its announcement to the records that reference it `[decision]`. It is unique enough without any coordination between tools: the tool draws it uniformly at random from the 2^64 − 1 non-zero values, as a module draws its instance nonce afresh (C-11), so no registry and no counter shared between tools or between invocations of one tool is needed `[decision]`. Among n windows the chance that any two share an identifier is at most n × (n − 1) / 2 / (2^64 − 1); for one million windows that is 499 999 500 000 / 18 446 744 073 709 551 615, about 2.7 × 10^-8, as arithmetic and not as a bound on how many windows a deployment opens `[decision]`. An identifier derived from the tool identity and a counter was not chosen: `window open` and `window close` are separate invocations of the tool (028b-09), so the counter would have to persist between them, while a random draw needs no state, and the close and an extension take the identifier from the stamps that carry it (028b-09, `window status`) `[decision]`. Zero is not a window identifier: a zeroed buffer is then never a valid announcement or close, as code 0 is never a control message (Hello, Control message type codes), and a record or a tool can write 0 for no window without naming a real one `[decision]`. The width is the stamp's, 64 bits (Regime stamp, Commissioning window section) `[decision]`.\n\n**Tool identity.** The commissioning tool is not a module and has no module id: the design gives module ids to modules (C-11), and the tool never takes part in a live data path (028a-01) `[decision]`. The announcement therefore names its tool by a tool identity of its own, 64 bits, the width of the module id and the instance nonce (C-11), every value valid `[decision]`. The tool writes the same value in every announcement of one window, across its invocations, so that a module can tell a repeat or an extension by the announcing tool from an announcement that only reuses the identifier (Receiver rules, rule 5) `[decision]`. Modules do not stamp it — the commissioning window section carries the identifier and the expiry only — and grant nothing by it, because v1 authenticates no control message (C-115); how the tool chooses and keeps the value is commissioning tooling's (Open item 3) `[decision]`.\n\n**Expiry time.** The expiry is an absolute instant, never a span counted from the announcement: every module stamps it verbatim (Regime stamp, Commissioning window section, Open item 11), 028b-09 expects `window status` to show the same expiry at every module (AC 1), and an announcement that arrives late, twice or re-sent then names the same instant at every module, where a span would end the window later at a module that received it later `[decision]`. Its clock is network time, the one time scale the design gives every module that follows the holder: position is network time counted from a domain epoch origin (timeline.md, Domain line and position map), and a module's local monotonic time or wall clock is not shared, so an expiry on either would name different instants at different modules `[decision]`. Its unit is the nanosecond, the unit in which timeline.md counts network time and the epoch origin `origin_ns` (timeline.md, The epoch origin), so the test of 007b-12, the window still stamped 1 ns before the expiry and no longer at it (AC 2), is exact `[decision]`.\n\nNetwork time is a signed 64-bit nanosecond count (timeline.md, The epoch origin), and the field is a u64, the type of the stamped expiry (Regime stamp, Commissioning window section): its valid range is 0 to 2^63 − 1, the non-negative network times, on which the u64 and the i64 readings of the 8 bytes agree, so the stamp's verbatim copy has one meaning; a value of 2^63 or above names no network time an i64 can hold and is out of range (Validity rules) `[decision]`. 2^63 − 1 ns is about 292 years of network time, so the range bounds no window by its length; no constant bounds how long a window may be, and this section sets no maximum length (Open item 4) `[decision]`. An expiry before network time 0 cannot be written; whether network time can be negative on a v1 holder is not stated by timeline.md, which gives only the i64 range (Open item 5) `[decision]`. The tool computes the expiry as its network time at the announcement plus the length the operator states (028b-09: `window open --duration <d>`, with no default); the design does not say how the tool, which is not a module, reads network time (Open item 3) `[decision]`.\n\n### Window close\n\nThe window close, code 49 (Hello, Control message type codes), ends the window it names before its expiry (C-153). Little-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding (Alignment and padding); bytes 0 to 31 are the common control header, and the window identifier follows, nothing else (004-29, Work 2) `[decision]`:"

input x12 excerpt "Sync request and reply" "## Sync request and reply\n\nA follower estimates its offset from the holder with request/reply exchanges on the sync port: the follower sends a sync request to the holder, and the holder answers each request with one sync reply. The holder's monotonic clock defines network time (01-architecture.md § 2.3), and a reply carries what a follower needs to place itself on the domain line: the holder's two timestamps of the exchange, the timeline epoch with its origin, and the holder's identity `[decision]`. This section fixes both layouts, the timestamps' unit and clock, the decisions this ticket owns, and every invalid form with its outcome `[decision]`.\n\n### Exchange rules\n\nThe exchange is stateless: the reply echoes the request's own send timestamp verbatim, so the holder answers each request from that request alone and keeps no per-request state, and a follower pairs a reply with its request by the echoed value, read on its own clock `[decision]`. A stale or duplicate reply is therefore a valid exchange with an honestly large round trip — its echoed send timestamp is old, so the round trip the follower computes from it is long — and never an invalid form; the follower's exchange filtering, which this specification does not define, decides what a long round trip is worth `[decision]`. Nothing in either message names an exchange: the holder's per-module values in a reply — its clock, its module id, its current epoch and origin, its message counter — are the holder's own state, the same whichever request is being answered `[decision]`.\n\nSync messages travel by UDP unicast over IPv4 (C-100) at DSCP CS6 (48) (C-13): the follower sends its request to the holder's sync port, and the holder sends the reply to the source address and port the request came from, which is all the addressing a stateless reply needs `[decision]`. The class-selector codepoints are the 'xxx000' set (RFC 2474, § 4.2.2.1 The Class Selector Codepoints), CS6 being 110000 `[standard]`. Neither message carries a DSCP field: the holder records the DSCP it observes on each follower's requests on its clock thread (C-188) and reports it in its regime stamp (C-152), in the section 004-28 lays out `[decision]`.\n\nThe request rate is behaviour, never a field: a follower sends 50 requests per second (C-36), and the holder accepts 10 to 200 requests per second from each follower (C-112) `[decision]`. Requests beyond 200 per second from one follower are dropped before any work is done and counted per follower in the holder's regime stamp (C-204); that drop is not a rejection of a malformed message, it increments no counter of the closed enumeration, and its counter is laid out by 004-28, so neither message carries a rate field `[decision]`. How the per-follower entries of C-152 and C-204 identify a follower is 004-28's to fix; the request adds no identity field for it `[decision]`.\n\n### Authentication reservation\n\nSync messages carry the authentication reservation of C-12 — scheme 8 bits, message counter 64 bits, tag 128 bits — in both the request and the reply, at the same offsets in both, with the v1 values of C-115: scheme 0 (none), tag 128 zero bits, and a live counter `[decision]`. This closes R11 for sync messages; the receiver outcomes are those of Reserved fields, Authentication reservation (C-12): a non-zero scheme or a non-zero tag is dropped and counted under ReservedNonZero, and the counter never produces ReservedNonZero `[decision]`. Falsifier: a later authentication scheme cannot be added to sync messages without a major change — for example a scheme that needs more than the 128-bit tag, or a field the reservation does not hold — in which case this decision is wrong and the reservation's shape is reopened by epic 004 `[decision]`.\n\n**Why carry it.** Three arguments decide it, in order of weight `[decision]`:\n\n1. Adding it later is a major change by construction. Both messages are fixed-size, with no length prefix and no optional part, and a receiver rejects every other datagram size under BadLength (Validity rules below); a field added after v1 changes that fixed size, so every v1 receiver rejects the new message, and by Versioning, Minor and major changes, a change an older receiver can neither parse nor skip is a major one. Leaving the reservation out would make the ticket's falsifier true on the day the first scheme arrives; carrying it, a scheme fills fields that already exist at fixed offsets with the message unchanged in shape, so no existing field moves or widens `[decision]`.\n2. A forged reply is the most damaging forgery on the medianet. In v1 nothing authenticates a reply: one forged with the holder's module id and the domain passes every rule below. Its timestamps bias the follower's offset estimate, and its epoch, if it differs from the follower's current one and echoes a recent send timestamp, is taken as the holder's new epoch (Timeline epoch and holder identity below), after which every source of that module announces a switch and restarts its session (01-architecture.md § 2.2). The sync reply is therefore the first message a later scheme must cover, and the reservation is what lets it `[decision]`.\n3. The cost is small. The reservation is 25 bytes per message (200 bits). At the holder, at most 64 followers (C-35) each sending 50 requests per second (C-36) make 3 200 requests in and 3 200 replies out per second; the reservation adds 25 × 3 200 = 80 000 bytes per second in each direction, 0.64 Mbit/s, and at the accepted ceiling of 200 per second per follower (C-112) 2.56 Mbit/s. Whole sync traffic at 50 per second, the 28 bytes of IPv4 and UDP headers included (Layer overview), is (74 + 28) × 3 200 × 8 = 2 611 200 bit/s per direction, about 2.6 Mbit/s — an eighth of one 6-channel stream's 21.1 Mbit/s (C-21). The holder's serving work grows by a 25-byte copy and two zero comparisons per message, with no cryptography in v1, so the holder-serving-lateness falsifier of C-35 is not brought nearer `[decision]`.\n\nThe counter is live in sync messages as in control messages (C-115): each module increments one sync-message counter by one for every sync message it sends, request or reply, and that counter is module state, not per-request state. In v1 no receiver rule depends on its value — liveness on the sync layer is judged on the replies themselves (C-37) — and a later scheme finds its replay counter already on the wire `[decision]`. The header keeps the field order ticket 004-16 names for the common control header — magic, version, domain, message type, authentication reservation — so one header parser can serve both layers; if 004-16 lays its header out differently, the sync layer keeps this layout, which no control parser reads `[decision]`.\n\n### Request\n\nLittle-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding for alignment (Alignment and padding); offsets are byte distances from the first byte of the UDP payload. The request carries the common header and the follower's send timestamp, then explicit padding to the reply's size `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 1 = sync request (Message type codes) | 1 only |\n| 7 | 1 | u8 | Authentication scheme (C-12); 0 = none in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Message counter (C-12): live (C-115), incremented by one for every sync message the follower sends | any 64-bit value |\n| 16 | 16 | u128 | Authentication tag (C-12): 128 zero bits in v1 (C-115) | 0 only |\n| 32 | 8 | u64 | Send timestamp: the follower's local monotonic clock in nanoseconds when it sends the request; opaque to the holder, which echoes it verbatim (Timestamps) | any 64-bit value |\n| 40 | 34 | pad | Padding: brings the request to the reply's size, the room the reply's receive and send timestamps, holder module id, epoch origin and timeline epoch take; senders write zero (Reserved fields, general rule) | 0 only |\n"

input x13 excerpt "Receiver report" "## Receiver report\n\nThe receiver report is a consumer's account of one bundle to the bundle's producer: the consumer's data thread sends one report per bundle every 100 ms (C-40), carrying per member the eleven counters of C-159 and the observed DSCP, per bundle the socket and interface drop counters, and the consumer's current A (C-198) `[decision]`. The v1 measurement layer has exactly two message kinds, this report and the one-way probe with its request and reply (One-way probe below); there is no third `[decision]`. The report is also the producer's only evidence that its consumer is alive: a producer times out after 2 s without receiver reports (C-41), which is behaviour, not a field `[decision]`.\n\n### Transport\n\nReports travel by UDP unicast over IPv4 (C-100) at DSCP CS5 (40) (C-13), from the consumer to the reverse port its producer gave in the admission handshake; 004-18 lays out that port and its negotiation `[decision]`. The report is unicast only, never multicast, and there is no query message: a third party sees stream health in the regime stamps, where producer and consumer each publish per-connection counters (C-47, C-159) in the sections 004-25 lays out `[decision]`. The sender sets the IPv4 don't-fragment bit, as on every packet of the protocol (ADR 01) `[decision]`. Forward media packets carry no per-receiver state, and round-trip closure uses this measurement path (rule 8) `[decision]`.\n\nNo field carries a rate, an interval or a timeout: one report per bundle every 100 ms (C-40) and the producer's 2 s timeout (C-41) are behaviour of the state machines of epics 005 and 006, and a change of A travelling upstream one hop per report, with each fan-in that inherited the old value re-aligning (C-198, C-186), is behaviour too; this section fixes only what the fields mean `[decision]`.\n\n### Size bound of the measurement layer\n\nNo landed rule bounds measurement messages: rule 5 of Field-table format and C-17 are written for control messages, and the Layer overview states no bound for the measurement layer `[decision]`. This section adopts the same bound for both measurement messages: every receiver report and every probe fits one unfragmented datagram on the fallback path, at most 1 252 bytes of UDP payload (C-06, C-100) `[decision]`. The reason is ADR 01: IP fragmentation is forbidden, and a connection may run on the 1 280-byte fallback path (C-06), so a report that did not fit there could not be sent on such a connection at all, and its producer would time out (C-41) on a healthy stream `[decision]`.\n\n### Authentication reservation\n\nThe receiver report and the one-way probe do not carry the authentication reservation of C-12: neither message has a scheme, a message counter or a tag field, in v1 `[decision]`. Falsifier: a later authentication scheme is to cover the receiver report or the one-way probe, which requires ADR 22's exclusion of the data plane to be revised, and the scheme then cannot be added without a major change; in that case this decision is wrong and epic 004 reopens both layouts `[decision]`.\n\n**Why not carry it.** Four arguments decide it, in order of weight `[decision]`:\n\n1. ADR 22 settles the scope of the reserved scheme: \"The data plane is unauthenticated, in v1 and in the reserved scheme\". Both measurement messages are data-plane messages: C-198 places the report's carriage of A \"on the data plane\", the consumer's data thread sends it (01-architecture.md § 3.6), and the probe rides the media class EF (46) to measure the media path (C-13). Wire space in them would be space that no planned scheme fills `[decision]`.\n2. A forged report could do harm, and that is stated plainly: one carrying the consumer's module id could keep a producer sending after its consumer died (C-41 never fires), carry a changed A that makes every fan-in that inherited A re-align (C-198, C-186), or falsify the counters the producer publishes in its regime stamp. v1 guarantees protection against accident, not against attack (ADR 22): a report from a foreign domain, for another source's module id, or from a reporter with no admitted connection for the bundle its rows name is dropped and counted (Validity rules below), which is the protection the media layer has (only admitted peers are parsed, 01-architecture.md § 6.4) `[decision]`.\n3. Cost is not the argument: the reservation is 25 bytes per message, at one report per bundle per 100 ms 250 bytes per second per bundle, and the report fits the bound with or without it (Maximum size below) `[decision]`.\n4. Adding it later is a major change, because both messages have sizes their tables fix and a receiver rejects every other size under BadLength (Validity rules below); that is exactly the case the falsifier names, and the falsifier ties it to the revision of ADR 22 that would have to come first `[decision]`.\n\nThe Reserved fields section stays true as it stands: its C-12 rows name control and sync messages only, and the measurement messages carry no reserved field other than padding, which follows that section's general rule `[decision]`.\n\n### Fixed part\n\nLittle-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding for alignment (Alignment and padding); offsets are byte distances from the first byte of the UDP payload. Bytes 0 to 6 are the common header the sync messages start with — magic, version, domain, message type — and byte 7 is the member count, so bytes 0 to 7 are the part every measurement message starts with; the fixed part is 38 bytes `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 1 = receiver report (Message type codes below) | 1 only |\n| 7 | 1 | u8 | Member count: how many member rows follow the fixed part, one per bundle member admitted to this consumer (C-08) | 1 to 32 |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Bundle identity: the module id (C-11) of the bundle's source, the producer the report goes to; with the rows' stream numbers it names exactly one bundle (Bundle identity and member rows) | any 64-bit value; a producer accepts only its own module id |\n| 16 | 8 | u64 | Reporter identity: the module id (C-11) of the consumer that sends the report (Bundle identity and member rows) | any 64-bit value; a producer keys the connection by this identity with the bundle the first row's stream number names, and accepts only a module admitted for that bundle |"

input x14 excerpt "One-way probe" "## One-way probe\n\nThe one-way probe is a request and its reply between two modules that share an admitted connection, in either direction: either end, producer or consumer, sends a request on demand, and the other end answers each request with one reply `[decision]`. Four instants close the exchange: the requester's send time, the responder's receive and send times, and the requester's own receive time of the reply, which never travels, as in the sync exchange `[decision]`. It is not the path-MTU probe pair of the admission handshake (C-116), which is a pair of control messages that 004-27 lays out (Path-MTU probe pair) `[decision]`.\n\n### Exchange rules\n\nProbes travel by UDP unicast over IPv4 (C-100) at DSCP EF (46) (C-13), the media class, so they cross the network in the queue the media packets use and measure the media path `[decision]`. A consumer sends its requests to the reverse port its producer gave in the admission handshake (004-18); a producer sends its requests to the source address and port the consumer's reports come from; a reply goes to the source address and port of its request, which is all the addressing a stateless reply needs `[decision]`. The sender sets the IPv4 don't-fragment bit (ADR 01) `[decision]`. A probe is sent on demand: no field carries a rate, and any limit on how often a module probes or answers is behaviour, which this section does not fix `[decision]`.\n\nThe responder is stateless: the reply echoes the request's requester identifier and send timestamp verbatim, so the responder answers each request from that request alone, and the requester pairs a reply with its request by the echoed values, as the sync exchange does (Sync request and reply, Exchange rules) `[decision]`. A stale or duplicate reply is therefore a valid exchange with an honestly large round trip, never an invalid form `[decision]`.\n\n**Matching fields.** A reply matches when its echoed requester identifier is the receiving module's own module id and its responder module id is the module id of a module that shares an admitted connection with the receiving module `[decision]`. A reply that does not match was meant for another module, or comes from a module that is no peer: it is dropped and counted under UnadmittedSource, as is a request whose requester identifier names a module that shares no admitted connection with the responder; UnadmittedSource's Layers cell names the measurement layer and its meaning names these cases (Rejection reasons) `[decision]`.\n\n### Request\n\nLittle-endian (Byte order), packed with no padding for alignment (Alignment and padding); offsets are byte distances from the first byte of the UDP payload. The request carries the common header, the requester's identity and its send timestamp, then explicit padding to the reply's size `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; v1 packs 1.0 as 0x0100 (004-04) | major 1, any minor (Versioning, Receiver behaviour); senders write 0x0100 |\n| 4 | 2 | u16 | Domain id (C-11); 0 is the unconfigured domain | 1 to 65535; 0 = unconfigured |\n| 6 | 1 | u8 | Message type: 2 = one-way probe request (Receiver report, Message type codes) | 2 only |\n| 7 | 1 | pad | Padding: senders write zero (Reserved fields, general rule) | 0 only |\n| 8 | 8 | u64 | Requester identifier: the requester's module id (C-11), echoed by the reply | any 64-bit value; a responder answers only a module that shares an admitted connection with it |\n| 16 | 8 | i64 | Send timestamp: the requester's network time in nanoseconds when it sends the request (What the probe measures) | any 64-bit value |\n| 24 | 24 | pad | Padding: brings the request to the reply's size, the room the reply's responder module id and its two timestamps take; senders write zero (Reserved fields, general rule) | 0 only |\n\n### Reply\n\nSame conventions as the request; bytes 0 to 6 are the common header and byte 7, padding in the request, carries the responder's clock state; the echoed fields sit at the request's offsets, so a responder may build the reply over the request's own bytes, and the padding's room carries the responder's values `[decision]`:\n\n| Offset (bytes) | Width (bytes) | Type | Meaning | Valid range |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | 2 | u16 | Magic 0x4d4e, the ASCII letters M and N, fixed by 004-04 | 0x4d4e only |\n| 2 | 2 | u16 | Protocol version, major in the high byte (bits 15..8), minor in the low byte; input x15 excerpt "Validity rules" "## Validity rules\n\nThis section consolidates the invalid forms that the message sections of 004-06 to 004-20 and 004-24 to 004-29 state, one matrix row per message type in scope and one column per invalid-form class of ticket 004-21, and closes the holes the consolidation found by adding each missing rule to the message's own section `[decision]`. The message sections stay the authority for their rows; a cell here states what those rows, the shared rows of Versioning and Reserved fields, and the rule order below already say, and names the row it summarises by its section `[decision]`.\n\n### Uniform outcome\n\nEvery invalid form of every message in scope has one required outcome, the one system criterion AC-23 states in 03-acceptance-criteria.md — \"No crash, no state change; each rejected packet counted per input and per reason; version mismatch produces a named event\" — and the message sections give it: the datagram is dropped, or ignored for domain 0, which is the same drop counted under its own reason; it is counted once under one reason of the closed enumeration, keyed by (input, reason) when it matches an admitted input and by (socket, reason) when it matches none (Rejection reasons, Counting model); the rejection causes no state change; and a VersionMismatch also raises the named VersionMismatch event, so a version mismatch is never a silent drop (Versioning, Receiver behaviour; rule 12 of the epic file, doc/design/implementation/004-Wire-specification.md) `[decision]`. A content rejection drops the slice the content belongs to and counts each of its packets once, as BadChecksum does (Content messages, Validity rules) `[decision]`.\n\nTwo merged rules depart from \"no state change\", because a rejection there discards state that earlier, valid datagrams built: the regime stamp's disagreement rows — \"drop the datagram and every section held for that stamp version, the held complete stamp included, and count once under BadLength\" (Regime stamp, Validity rules) — and the manifest's — \"A manifest that breaks a rule below is dropped whole — every section of it held so far\" (Manifest, Validity rules), its disagreeing-section rows included. One forged or faulty datagram can therefore discard a peer's complete stamp, a stamp version being reassembled, or a handshake's manifest in progress, v1 authenticating no control message (C-115). Both are reported below as contradicting AC-23, and the specification keeps the merged rules meanwhile `[decision]`.\n\nForms that are not rejections — a skip by length, an identical repeat, a message well formed but judged by a state machine against per-peer or per-handshake state — are outside this matrix: they are counted under no reason, and what they do is governed by the rules of their own sections, not by AC-23's outcome `[decision]`.\n\n### Rule order\n\nOne order holds for every message: the rows of each validity table run in the order of the table, a row reads only bytes an earlier row has shown to exist, and the first row that applies decides, so each datagram is counted under one reason only — on the media layer, each packet once, either by a per-packet row or, if it passes them all, by the slice's checksum or content rows `[decision]`:\n\n1. **The magic and the version first.** TooShort for a datagram too small for the two leading fields (under 4 bytes on the control, sync and measurement layers; under the 16-byte packet header on the media layer), then BadMagic, then VersionMismatch on the major alone, before any other field is read (Versioning, The magic and the version fields) `[decision]`.\n2. **The layer's shared rows next, in the order of the message section's own table.** Each section fixes where its size, domain, type and oversize rows sit among themselves — the sync layer judges its one fixed size before the domain, the control layer judges the common header's 32 bytes before the domain and places each message's own size rows in that message's table — and the first row that applies decides `[decision]`.\n3. **Within one datagram, rows decided from its own bytes, or from the receiver's own module id and role, before rows that need per-peer or per-handshake state; rows on a joined payload after the reassembly that joins it.** A reassembled slice, a joined manifest and a complete stamp version are judged once joined, after the rows of each datagram that carried them. The reserved fields and every per-message row of a section's table run before the rows that read the discovery map, an admitted connection, the follower's current epoch, the held sections of a manifest or stamp, or the outstanding probes; the one exception is the media packet header's table, which keeps the order it had on main — its source, stream and epoch rows before its reserved-bit and flag rows — because that order is merged text, and the audit changes no outcome of it; 009-04 agrees that nothing beyond the header is read first — \"The payload beyond the header is not touched\" — and the order of the header's own rows against its lookup is handed to 009-04 below `[decision]`.\n4. **Shared rows before per-message rows.** Where a section has shared rows and per-message rows (Election messages, Admission messages), the shared rows run first, as those sections state `[decision]`.\n5. **The media layer, across its tables.** A media packet is judged table by table in this order, each table in its own row order, and the tables of Media packet header, Slice header, Announcements, Measurement extension and Checksum keep the row order they had, with two exceptions stated in Slice header and Announcements `[decision]`:\n   (a) the Media packet header's table: under 16 bytes, TooShort; the magic, BadMagic; the version's major, VersionMismatch with its event; another non-zero domain, ForeignDomain; domain 0, UnconfiguredDomain; no such stream for the pinned source, UnknownStream; no admitted connection for the source, UnadmittedSource; a timeline epoch other than the current one, WrongEpoch; reserved bits of byte 15 or of the flags, ReservedNonZero; a gap slice with a payload or a presence flag, BadLength;\n   (b) the Slice header's per-packet rows: a datagram of 16 to 37 bytes, or a non-gap packet without its count byte at offset 38, BadLength; packet count 0, BadLength — the count before the index, because with a count of 0 every index lies outside it; packet index at or above the packet count, BadPacketIndex; frames 0, BadLength;\n   (c) a gap packet that has passed (a) and (b) is accepted: it is exactly its 38 header bytes, so it skips every row that reads beyond them — the announcement container, the announcements, the measurement extension, the checksum and the content rows — and is judged by no row of steps (d) to (g) `[decision]`;\n   (d) for a packet of a non-gap slice, the Announcements table in its order: a packet that ends inside an announcement's type and length bytes, BadLength; a code outside 0 to 3 skipped by its length; a length that runs past the packet, BadLength; a length other than 10 for a code 0 to 3, BadLength; a non-zero payload in code 0, 1 or 3, ReservedNonZero; a position not in the future, a type twice in one packet, a count above 4, the flag and the count disagreeing, BadLength;\n   (e) the measurement extension's bytes missing or a hop count above 64, BadLength (Measurement extension); in the last packet, too few bytes left for the checksum, BadLength (Checksum);\n   (f) across the packets of one slice: a packet count that disagrees with another packet's, BadPacketIndex (Slice header);\n   (g) on the reassembled slice: a checksum mismatch or an identity byte that differs between packets, BadChecksum (Checksum); then the content rules, and the frames against the audio length, BadLength (Content messages; Slice header) `[decision]`.\n\nThe TooShort threshold differs per layer as merged, 16 bytes on the media layer and 4 bytes elsewhere, and both readings meet the enumeration's meaning — fewer bytes than the message's fixed minimum, dropped before any field is read — because the Media packet header section takes the whole 16-byte header as the media message's fixed minimum, while the control, sync and measurement sections take the two leading fields as theirs and judge a datagram between 4 bytes and its fixed part under BadLength; the difference changes only which reason counts a short datagram, never whether it is dropped `[decision]`. An unassigned or unexpected message type is BadLength on the control, sync and measurement layers alike, and a new message type is not a minor change: a v1 receiver drops it (Election messages, Why two messages) `[decision]`.\n\n### Outcomes that differ from main\n\nThe order above was built to keep every outcome of main's tables and to change one only where main's order made a row unreachable or merged text required it; this list names every reordered case with its outcome, changed or unchanged `[decision]`:\n\n- A packet count of 0, with any packet index: the outcome changed, from BadPacketIndex to BadLength, because in main's order the index row came first and always holds at a count of 0, which made the merged \"packet count = 0\" row, BadLength, unreachable; the reorder puts the count first, as 004-08's row and 004-09's note (Announcements, Why BadLength) intended `[decision]`.\n- Frames 0 together with a packet index at or above a non-zero packet count: the outcome is unchanged, still BadPacketIndex, because the index row still comes before the frames row, as on main `[decision]`.\n- A packet from an unadmitted source, or of an unknown stream or a wrong epoch, that also breaks a reserved-bit, gap, slice-header, announcement or extension row: the outcome is unchanged, still UnadmittedSource, UnknownStream or WrongEpoch, because the Media packet header keeps its order on main and its table runs before every table beyond the packet header, which agrees with 009-04's \"The payload beyond the header is not touched\" `[decision]`.\n- A datagram of 16 to 37 bytes with domain 0 or another non-zero domain: the outcome is unchanged, still UnconfiguredDomain or ForeignDomain, because the short-slice-header row runs after the whole packet header table, whose domain rows read only bytes the 16-byte TooShort row has shown to exist `[decision]`.\n- An announcement of an unknown type code whose length runs past the packet: the outcome is unchanged, still skipped by its length, because the skip row still comes before the length-overrun row, as on main; what follows such a skip — the skipped announcement ends beyond the packet, and the skip row says only that the receiver \"reads on with the next\" — is stated by no merged row, as on main, and is handed on below rather than decided here `[decision]`."
